tip: Like the "e" in "bed" — sometimes held a little longer.
Round your lips as if to say "o," but say "e" — close to the "ur" in British "her," without the r-sound.
Round your lips as if to say "u," but say "i" — like French "u" in "tu."
Two different sounds, depending on what comes right before it.

variants.label: After a, o, u, au (the "ach-Laut")
variants.tip: A harsh sound from the back of the throat — like Scottish "loch."

variants.label: After e, i, ä, ö, ü, and consonants (the "ich-Laut")
variants.tip: A softer, hissier sound — tongue near the roof of the mouth, like a whispered "h" in "huge."

tip: Usually a soft, gargled sound from the back of the throat — not a rolled or tapped "r." At the end of a word or syllable it often softens toward a vowel-like sound.
At the start of a word (or word part), the "s" shifts to an "sh" sound — "sp" becomes "shp," "st" becomes "sht."
Always "ts," like the end of English "cats" — never like English "z" in "zoo."
Usually like English "f" — except in some words borrowed from other languages, where it sounds like English "v."
Like English "y" in "yes" — not like English "j" in "jump."
